Executive summary

Sweetwater can turn its largest organizational buyers into a $20M to $30M a year named accounts business within two years by giving them a dedicated team of 10 to 20 account managers, led by one Director of Strategic Accounts who builds the plans, the standards, and the people.

Today these organizations buy from us one PO at a time. A park IT manager orders a QSYS Core, a church orders a camera, and nobody on our side sees the bigger plan behind the purchase. The named accounts team changes that. Each account manager owns a short list of organizations, learns their long term goals and decision makers, and builds a written technology plan and budget with them. Designers and Sweetwater Commercial come in as support, and the account manager stays the primary point person.

Compensation for the role would be set by Sweetwater. The plan includes market examples from AV integrators and manufacturers, and under those examples the role costs roughly 1% to 2% of team revenue once the team reaches $20M. The two year on ramp is real, so year one is about choosing the right organizations, hiring the first account managers, and delivering the first account plans.

The role

The Director of Strategic Accounts (the role proposed here) owns the named accounts strategy and the team that carries it out, and stays hands on with the largest organizations while the team ramps.

Title options (still to be decided; this plan uses Director of Strategic Accounts, a common market title; QSYS uses Senior Director of Strategic Accounts for the leader of its largest accounts)

Title What it signals
Director of Named Accounts Clear scope, matches the named accounts language
Director of Strategic Accounts Common market title, easiest to benchmark pay against
Head of Enterprise Accounts Places the team inside Commercial after the restructure

Mission. Make Sweetwater an extension of each named organization’s team, not just a vendor. We understand their goals, plan their technology years ahead, support what we sell, and beat the prices they were paying across many suppliers.

Responsibilities

  • Choose which organizations become named accounts, and match each one to the right account manager.
  • Hire, coach, and develop account managers so they can find the real decision makers and the vision behind every PO.
  • Build account plans with each account manager: goals, stakeholders, ten year technology roadmap, budget strategy, and a revenue funnel.
  • Create schematic level designs and system standards that hand off cleanly to a designer or to Sweetwater Commercial.
  • Stay the senior relationship for the biggest accounts, such as Six Flags corporate.
  • Report pipeline, revenue, and account health to leadership on a set cadence.

What the role is not. It is not a designer role and not an installation project manager role. Detailed design, engineering, and install move to designers and Commercial, with the account manager coordinating.

Location and travel. The Director of Strategic Accounts continues to live and work remotely, traveling to Fort Wayne no more than once a month to meet with the team. Travel to client sites follows the needs of the largest accounts. Account managers also need the ability to travel occasionally to meet with larger clients.

Operating model

The account manager owns the relationship and the plan; designers and Sweetwater Commercial deliver the systems; the director sets standards and clears the path.

  1. Find the goal behind the order. Goals come from senior leadership (executives, senior pastors, elders, boards), not only from the IT manager or tech director. We bring the worship pastor or park IT lead into that conversation instead of stepping over them.
  2. Write it down. Turn the conversation into a documented account plan: goals, standards, decision makers, and what gets replaced over the next ten years.
  3. Do the hard thing first. Infrastructure, structured cabling, network, and IP scheme come first so later Dante, QLAN, SACN…etc systems and console swaps are simpler sales.
  4. Hand off cleanly. The account manager passes a schematic design to a designer (white glove projects) or to Sweetwater Commercial (faster, standard projects).
  5. Support what we sell. For every system type, someone on the team owns it, holds the certifications, and can answer the call.
  6. Win on price too. These organizations buy from many places because price matters at a corporate level (churches are corporations too). A single trusted supplier with better pricing removes that reason.

Example: Six Flags. Six Flags corporate is moving every park from aging Media Matrix audio to QSYS, using Six Flags Over Texas as the template, and the merged company now runs from Arlington. Parks still buy semi independently, so a PO for a Core Nano can be the wrong choice for a ride that really needs a Core 8 Flex for I/O with older Crown amps, or a better path such as CX-Q amps on QLAN or a QSYS Dante license with existing LEA amps. An account manager who knows the corporate plan asks the right questions and sells the right system. Box sales alone could reach $5M+ a year just for Six Flags if we hold all of their business.

Example: Gateway Church. Gateway runs ten campuses on shared standards (Meyer, DiGiCo, Waves, MA consoles, Martin profiles, Resi between campuses) so staff can move between them and services sound the same. Knowing their goals and their staffing changes let us recently demo auto tracking Sony PTZ cameras as an option to manned follow cam systems. Manned systems start above $50K plus operators which Gateway may not be able to support long term with its restructuring. That moves us from salesperson to extension of their team.

Where we create value for Sweetwater. The team is the point of entry for B2B accounts that Commercial cannot win alone, a showcase for high end capability, and a feeder of steady box sales once standards are set.

Team structure and system ownership

Ten account managers is potentially how large the team could be, growing toward 20, with each one owning a book of $2M to $4M a year and one primary technology specialty.

Account managers do not need to be experts in everything. Each picks the platform they love, goes deep, then branches into what it touches: QSYS leads to Dante, Dante leads to network design and IP schemes. They do not have to build the network, but they must speak to it well enough to plan it.

Specialty lane Core platforms Typical accounts Certifications to pursue
Distributed audio and control QSYS, QLAN, CXQ amps, 70 volt Theme parks, campuses, municipalities QSYS Level 1 to 3
Audio networking and infrastructure Dante, Networks, structured cable Every account Dante Level 1 to 3, AVIXA/Netgear network credential
Live sound and consoles Meyer, L-Acoustics, DiGiCo, Yamaha, Waves…etc Multisite churches, venues Manufacturer console/PA training, Ease
Lighting MA Lighting, Ovation, Martin…etc Churches, venues, theme park shows MA and Martin product training
Video and streaming Broadcast Video, LED walls Multisite churches, corporate, production Manufacturer training and real world experience

Reporting lines. Account managers are salaried employees who report to the director. Designers and Sweetwater Commercial stay in their own teams and support named accounts through an agreed handoff. Named division owns the relationship, we all own the success.

Revenue opportunity

Ten account managers at $2M to $4M each is a $20M to $40M business; the plan is to hit $20M to $30M by the end of year two and treats anything above that as upside.

Year Account managers (end of year) Average book per account manager Team revenue Notes
Year 1 (2027) 4 to 5 ramping $8M to $12M Existing named accounts
Year 2 (2028) 10 $2M to $3M $20M to $30M Target range for the plan
Year 3 (2029) 12 to 15 $2.5M to $3.2M $35M to $45M Standards in place, repeat box sales grow
Full potential 20 $2M to $4M $40M to $80M Long range ceiling, not a commitment

Where the revenue comes from

  • Theme parks and attractions. Six Flags alone could be $5M+ a year in box sales with all of their business, across a park wide QSYS migration. Disney, Herschend, Sea World are all on the table as well.
  • Multisite churches. Standardized campuses mean every new campus or refresh repeats the same bill of materials.
  • Municipalities, schools, and athletic venues. Long budget cycles reward the team that helped write the plan.
  • Corporate campuses. Repeatable conference and training room standards across sites.

Account load per account manager

Each account manager should plan to hold about 50 named accounts, which builds in 30% headroom because not every account will double.

Assumption: a typical named account spends $50K to $100K a year with us today, and the program can roughly double that to $100K to $200K. The 30% headroom covers accounts that grow slower, stall, or churn.

  • Deep planning on the top 25%. Full account plans, ten year roadmaps, and budget strategy go to the top 25% of each book, about 15 accounts per account manager. The rest get a lighter standard plan and steady service, which keeps a book of 50 accounts manageable.
  • Team scale. Ten account managers at 50 accounts each means about 500 named accounts. The year one target list is the start, and purchase history will show how deep that pool really is.
  • Question. Is it possible to effectively run 100 or more accounts in this role? Possibly at first, maybe not long term with the current business strategy.

Cost of the role and return

The plan has two kinds of roles with different costs: one Director of Strategic Accounts (the role proposed here) and the account managers who manage the accounts day to day.

Director of Strategic Accounts. Pay would be set by Sweetwater with additional discussion of targets and role expectations. Across the market examples in the compensation section, the role costs roughly $250K to $390K a year at $20M of team revenue, about 1% to 2% of revenue.

Account managers. Account managers are salaried employees who help manage the named accounts, most of them moving over from Sweetwater sales engineer roles. They are paid a salary plus commission on their individual performance. The specific numbers will be set separately by the appropriate team based on experience.

Year one guarantee. Each sales engineer who moves into an account manager role is guaranteed at least their prior year’s total earnings for the first 12 months while books build. After year one, pay can be negotiated by tenure and experience.

Whole team economics. At $25M of revenue and a 20% margin, the team produces about $5M of gross profit. The director’s pay would be a small part of that. Account manager pay, set separately, is the larger share of team cost, and finance will judge the total against gross profit. The plan works best when average books pass $3M per account manager.

The return Sweetwater should count

  • Incremental revenue. Business that was going to other suppliers, measured against each account’s spend before the program.
  • Protected revenue. Accounts like Six Flags that a competitor could take if no one owns the relationship.
  • Pull through. Standards and infrastructure done first make later console, lighting, and video sales simple Commercial orders.
  • Market credibility. A visible high end team helps Sweetwater be taken seriously across commercial AV.

Compensation: market examples

Compensation for the Director of Strategic Accounts would be set by Sweetwater. This section shows how AV integrators and manufacturers pay comparable roles, and a few structures that fit the named accounts model, as a starting point for that conversation.

Example structure

Structure How it works Example at $20M of team revenue (20% margin)
Base plus share of team gross profit $160K to $190K base, plus 5% of team gross profit about $360k+ based on team performance and actual margin

Considerations for pay structure

  • Pay on gross profit where possible. It ties the role to margin as well as volume, which protects Sweetwater when large accounts push on price. These accounts will likely run at or below a 20% margin.
  • Plan for the on ramp. Revenue builds over two years, so a year one floor or a larger share of base pay keeps the plan fair early on.
  • Room to grow. A step up in base after the team reaches a milestone, such as $15M, rewards proven results instead of setting a high number up front.

Action plan

Year one builds the foundation (target list, first hires, first account plans); year two scales to ten account managers and $20M+.

First 90 days

  • Settle the title, reporting line inside Commercial, and the comp plan in writing.
  • Agree on crediting rules with Commercial and the design team so shared work is paid fairly.
  • Build the target list: 15 to 25 organizations scored on annual AV spend, number of sites, and how much of their spend we capture today.
  • Pull each target’s last three years of Sweetwater purchases to set a baseline.
  • Pull prior year earnings for each sales engineer moving over to set their year one guarantee.
  • Write the account plan template: goals, decision makers, current standards, ten year roadmap, budget strategy, revenue funnel.
  • Complete the first two account plans: Six Flags corporate and Gateway Church (drafts in the appendix).
  • Pick the first two or three account managers (current SEs or designers who prefer relationships over pure design).

Rest of year one (2027)

  • Grow to 4 or 5 account managers, each with a specialty lane and a certification plan.
  • Deliver a written account plan for every named account.
  • Lead with infrastructure: propose network and cabling standards at the top accounts first.
  • Launch a monthly account review with each account manager and a quarterly report to leadership.
  • Build standard system packages (for example, a QSYS ride audio kit) that Commercial can quote fast.
  • Hit $8M to $12M of team revenue.

Year two (2028)

  • Reach 10 account managers with average books moving toward $2M to $3M.
  • Add a senior account manager as team lead once the team passes 12.
  • Expand into new verticals based on what year one proved.
  • Hit $20M to $30M of team revenue and reset the comp plan with real margin data.

In the short term success is the right organizations in active conversation; in the long term it is written plans turning into revenue and margin.

Risks and open questions

  • Slow on ramp. Two years before full payoff; a pay structure that accounts for the ramp keeps the plan fair while revenue builds.
  • Margin pressure. Winning on price with large buyers can thin margins; paying the bonus on gross profit protects Sweetwater.
  • Crediting fights. Busy designers want a piece before helping, and account managers paid on their own books will want clear rules when accounts overlap. Crediting rules must be set before launch.
  • Talent. Few SEs combine deep tech knowledge with executive relationship skills; some designers will prefer to stay in craft roles. The year one earnings guarantee removes the risk of a pay cut for the sales engineers we want most.
  • Burnout in Commercial. Many system types and back end platforms land on one team; standard packages reduce that load.

Open questions

  • What is the title (doesn’t matter) and where does the team sit after the Commercial restructure?
  • What is Sweetwater’s real blended gross margin on these categories?
  • What does each target organization spend with us today, and in total?
  • How is credit split when two account managers or a designer share an account? Each account manager’s bonus depends on it.
  • Does the director keep a personal book of accounts, and if so, how is that paid?

Appendix: example account plans

These two plans show what an account manager delivers for a named account. They are built from current knowledge of each organization. Items marked “to confirm” need data or a conversation before the plan is final.

Snapshot. Six Flags and Cedar Fair have merged under the Six Flags name, and corporate headquarters moved from Charlotte, North Carolina to Arlington, Texas. Each park runs semi independently. Six Flags Over Texas is the template park for the company’s audio direction. Current annual spend with Sweetwater: to confirm. Potential box sales with all of their business: $5M+ a year.

The core problem: purchasing is siloed. At each park, IT buys some systems and Entertainment buys others, and the two teams often are not talking about overall strategy. Corporate sets direction, such as the move to QSYS, but parks carry it out one PO at a time. The result is gear that does not fit the bigger plan, duplicate spending, and systems that are hard to support. Our main goal is to bring IT, Entertainment, and corporate together around one long term strategy for their parks.

Their goals

  • Replace aging Media Matrix distributed audio across every park. Those systems are past the point of replacement parts and service, and the people who installed or understood them are often gone.
  • Standardize on QSYS company wide, using Six Flags Over Texas as the model.
  • Improve audio quality where it matters most to guests, without overspending where it does not.
  • Build systems that park teams can support long term.
  • Get better pricing by buying with a plan instead of piecemeal.

Who decides and who influences

Group What they buy or control What they care about
Corporate leadership Company wide standards, such as the move to QSYS Consistency, cost control, brand experience
Park IT managers Processors, networks, and much of the audio infrastructure Reliability, supportability, network security
Six Flags Entertainment Show and ride audio, content, and special effects Guest experience, creative flexibility, automation
Park presidents and leadership Park level budgets and project approval Guest satisfaction, uptime, budget

How we bring the teams together

  1. Map every park. Identify the IT manager, Entertainment lead, and park leader at each park, and who signs each kind of PO.
  2. Hold a joint planning session. Bring corporate, IT, and Entertainment into one room, starting at Six Flags Over Texas, to agree on goals and who owns what.
  3. Write one shared standards book. A single document covering processors, amplifiers, speakers, networks, and ride audio, so both teams buy to the same plan.
  4. Set up a shared review. Any audio purchase above an agreed size gets a quick check against the standards book before the PO goes out. We run this review with them.
  5. Meet quarterly. A standing planning meeting with all three groups to update the roadmap and budget.

Standards to propose: ride audio

Parks often order QSYS gear without the full picture. A clear standard keeps every park buying the right system the first time.

  • Core Nano only when the ride uses Dante based amps, since the Nano has no onboard I/O.
  • Core 8 Flex as the minimum when a ride reuses older Crown XTi or XLi amps.
  • CXQ amps on QLAN when a smaller ride can live on the existing park QSYS network instead of running standalone.
  • QSYS Dante license instead of a new core when the park already has Dante amps (such as LEA) or plans Dante wireless microphones.
  • Decide up front whether each ride needs its own redundant system or can run on the park network.
  • QSYS Touch Panel for ride control and operation.
  • Foot Pedal controlled operator microphone system

Speaker strategy

Six Flags Over Texas has started moving to higher end speakers and away from JBL. Six Flags Fiesta Texas has decided to stay with JBL. So speaker choice may stay a park by park decision, at least for now.

  • Short term: support each park’s choice, and document what each park uses and why.
  • Long term: run a structured manufacturer partnership process with several manufacturers, JBL and Community. Use Sweetwater purchasing to help negotiate pricing and best strategy. It’s not always about best product in these circumstances.
    • Each manufacturer presents its best project pricing and margin for a multiyear, multipark program. We pass the savings on to Six Flags.
    • Six Flags sees which manufacturer is the better long term partner: pricing, product fit for outdoor theme park use, support, training, and lead times.
    • The outcome is either one preferred speaker standard company wide or a clear tier system, such as a premium tier for flagship areas and a standard tier everywhere else.
  • Why this matters for Sweetwater: it moves us from quoting individual speaker orders to managing a multiyear program, with manufacturers investing in the relationship alongside us.

Infrastructure and network

  • Agree on network and IP standards for audio with park IT, so QSYS QLAN and Dante run reliably on park networks.
  • Lead with infrastructure on new projects so later processor and speaker upgrades are simple box sales. QSYS Core first, speaker upgrades and advanced programming second.

Ten year roadmap

Phase Focus
Year 1 Finish Six Flags Over Texas; hold the first joint planning session; publish the standards book and ride audio standard; audit Media Matrix systems at every park; launch the JBL and Community partnership process
Years 2 to 3 Migrate parks in priority order, starting with the systems closest to failure; settle the speaker standard or tiers; set network and IP standards for audio. Evaluate with SF leadership which parks are most mission critical.
Years 4 to 6 Extend QSYS to shows, attractions, and automation, such as launch tunnel zones and triggered ride elements
Years 7 to 10 Planned refresh of the earliest migrated parks, using the standards book. This includes QSYS upgrades, speaker replacement, and local installation labor support.

Budget strategy

  • Build a migration budget for each park (to confirm with each park), with IT and Entertainment spending shown side by side.
  • Phase spending over the roadmap so each park knows what is coming each year.
  • Set program pricing at the corporate level, supported by manufacturer partnership pricing, so parks stop buying piecemeal from many suppliers. Deliver this as a portal or a quarterly price book.
  • Explore a Six Flags portal with program pricing so park teams can order standard items quickly.
  • Plan for fright fest and holiday in the park needs before this peak season.

Current opportunities

  • New coaster audio at Six Flags Fiesta Texas, with multiple launch tunnel zones and triggered ride elements. Entertainment is excited about what QSYS automation makes possible.
  • Ride audio packages for upcoming projects at other parks.
  • Speaker replacements at Six Flags Over Texas as it moves to higher end speakers.

How we support them

  • A named QSYS owner on the team holds QSYS Level 1 to 3 certification, studies how Six Flags operates its systems, and is the first call for design/purchase questions.
  • A speaker and live sound specialist works with JBL and Community on design, tuning, and training. This can be the same person.
  • One account manager coordinates across IT, Entertainment, and corporate so nothing falls between the teams.

Risks

  • Silos stay in place. Mitigation: start with one park, show results, and use that success to bring other parks in.
  • Media Matrix failures force emergency buys. Mitigation: identify the systems most at risk first and keep replacement kits ready. Failed system recently happened at Fiesta Texas causing panic buying.
  • Staff turnover at the parks. Mitigation: the standards book and account plan keep knowledge on paper, not in one person’s head.

How we measure success

  • A standards book adopted by corporate, IT, and Entertainment.
  • Share of total park audio spend that comes through Sweetwater, measured against the year one baseline.
  • Number of parks with a migration plan and budget in place.
  • Fewer one off purchases that do not match the standard.

Next 90 days

  • Map the IT manager, Entertainment lead, and park leader at every park, plus decision makers at corporate.
  • Pull three years of Sweetwater purchase history across all parks to set a baseline, split by IT and Entertainment where possible.
  • Hold the first joint planning session at Six Flags Over Texas.
  • Publish the ride audio standard and share it with every park.
  • Open conversations with JBL and Community about a multipark partnership program.

Snapshot. Gateway Church runs ten campuses on shared technology and operating standards, so staff and volunteers can move between campuses and services look and sound the same everywhere. Current annual spend with Sweetwater: to confirm.

Their goals

  • The same experience at every campus, down to SPL and EQ, monitored in real time during services.
  • An inviting, low distraction environment: lyric banners and lighting instead of full LED walls, with simple graphics.
  • The ability to sync services across campuses in near real time.
  • Run services well with leaner weekend production teams as staffing changes.

Who decides and who influences

Group Role in decisions
Senior pastor, elders, and board Set the long term vision and budget
Worship pastors Shape the service experience; included in every conversation
Tech directors and campus engineers Run systems and carry out standards

Current standards

  • Audio: Meyer loudspeakers, DiGiCo consoles, and Waves servers at every campus.
  • Lighting: MA consoles with Martin profile moving spots as key lights, chosen for flexibility.
  • Campus links: Resi encoders and decoders on Dante, carrying up to 16 channels of MADI to sync campuses.

Ten year roadmap (draft)

Phase Focus
Year 1 Document the full standard; audit every campus for age and condition; agree on the replacement schedule
Years 2 to 3 Network and Dante infrastructure refresh where needed; begin camera automation and audition
Years 4 to 6 Console and loudspeaker refresh on schedule, keeping the standard consistent, reevaluate goals
Years 7 to 10 Next generation standard set with leadership, ready for new campuses

Budget strategy. Turn one off requests into a ten year capital plan per campus, so leadership sees AV spending years ahead and new campuses repeat a known bill of materials.

Current opportunities

  • Auto tracking Sony PTZ cameras. Manned follow cam systems start above $50K plus operators. AI tracking can deliver high quality IMAG with fewer operators and lower system cost. A demo has already sparked interest. Great for satellite campuses.
  • Standard campus refresh packages that repeat across all ten campuses (I.E. House Lights, Cameras, Wireless systems…etc.)

How we support them. Account manager specialties in live sound and consoles, lighting, and video, with a clear contact for each part of the standard.

Next 90 days

  • Meet senior leadership, together with the worship pastors, to confirm goals.
  • Pull purchase history across all campuses to set a baseline.
  • Document the current standard and campus by campus condition.
  • Follow up on the PTZ demo with a pilot proposal for one campus. Look for manufacturer buy-in.

Tools and deliverables

Example tool: Church AVL Budget Calculator

Strategic accounts need more than quotes. Planning tools help an organization see the size and shape of its AV investment before a formal design, and they keep Sweetwater at the center of that conversation. The team can build tools like this for each type of named account.

Built by Joe Milne for Sweetwater Integration, this tool gives a church a rough order of magnitude estimate for audio, video, lighting, acoustics, and network systems. It works from room size, the systems needed, and a quality tier, then adds labor, an optional contingency, estimated electrical loads, and conduit runs, and produces a summary the church can share with its leadership.

  • For named accounts: versions could be built for theme park rides and attractions, multisite church campuses, and municipal venues, using each account's own standards and program pricing.
  • Why it matters: it turns budget conversations into written plans, which is the core of the account plan for each organization.
Live tool below.

The live calculator is available in the online version of this plan.

Example deliverable: Heritage Park AVL Systems Guide

High end clients expect more than a finished install. This interactive operations manual was made for the Heritage Park Amphitheater. It gives the client quick start cards for everyday tasks, a page by page guide to the QSYS touch panel, audio, video, and lighting sections, a guide for visiting shows, troubleshooting that walks through questions step by step, and who to call for help. It is searchable and printable.

  • For named accounts: every major system handed over with a guide like this, built to the account's standards, so staff turnover does not mean lost knowledge.
  • Why it matters: it reduces support calls, protects the system, and shows the level of care that keeps an organization coming back.
